questions.explanation: With the default of 200, small data turns into many tiny tasks. AQE's partition coalescing (on by default) or a lower or 'auto' setting produces reasonably sized partitions. More partitions would only add overhead.

questions.question: After changing spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, how should an engineer tell whether performance actually improved?
choices: Run a different, smaller data set and compare its duration with the old job
Assume it improved, since higher partition counts are always faster
Look only at the cluster's CPU utilization while the job runs
Re-run the same workload and data, and compare metrics with the baseline
questions.explanation: Tuning is empirical: keep the workload and data the same, change one variable, and compare the Spark UI or query profile metrics and the run durations (the job run history helps here) against a baseline.

questions.question: An engineer runs spark.conf.set('spark.executor.memory', '16g') in a notebook on a running classic cluster, but the executors still OOM. Why?
choices: It is fixed when executors launch; set it in the cluster config and restart
spark.conf.set changes executor memory only for SQL cells, not Python cells
Executor memory can only be changed through spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
The value must be given in megabytes ('16384m'); gigabytes are ignored
questions.explanation: Settings such as spark.executor.memory and spark.driver.memory are read when the JVMs start, so changing them in a session has no effect. Runtime settings such as spark.sql.shuffle.partitions can be changed per session. On Databricks, choosing the instance type is usually how memory is controlled.

questions.question: A team has moved its notebooks to serverless compute and wants to keep tuning Spark configs. Which statement is true?
choices: Every Spark property, including spark.executor.memory, can be set with spark.conf.set
No Spark properties can be set at all on serverless compute
Only a few properties, such as spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, can be set
Only spark.default.parallelism and spark.driver.memory can be set
questions.explanation: Serverless compute supports a short list of Spark properties (spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, spark.sql.session.timeZone, spark.sql.ansi.enabled, spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes, spark.sql.legacy.timeParserPolicy, spark.databricks.execution.timeout). Infrastructure and memory are managed automatically.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a view and a materialized view in Unity Catalog?
choices: A view runs its query on every read; a materialized view stores refreshed results
Views can contain joins, but materialized views can only read a single table
Materialized views are temporary and disappear when the session ends
A view stores precomputed results; a materialized view runs its query each time it is read
questions.explanation: Standard views compute their results at query time over the current base data. Materialized views physically store the results (as Unity Catalog managed objects) and are refreshed on a schedule, on a trigger, or manually, which speeds up repeated BI queries.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a streaming table?
choices: A view that recomputes its full result over all source data whenever it is queried
A Delta table that incrementally processes each new source record exactly once
A table that can only be read with spark.readStream and never with SQL
A table that holds only the latest micro-batch and discards older data
questions.explanation: Streaming tables process data incrementally: each refresh reads only the rows that arrived since the last update and appends them. They suit ingestion and append-only transformations.

questions.question: A gold dataset aggregates revenue per day by joining several silver tables that receive updates and deletes. Many dashboards read it. Which object fits best?
choices: A materialized view
A streaming table
A temporary view
An external table loaded with COPY INTO
questions.explanation: Materialized views suit aggregations and joins over sources that change through updates and deletes, and serve many downstream readers. They refresh incrementally when possible and otherwise fully. Streaming tables assume append-only sources.

questions.question: Which statement creates a materialized view that refreshes every day at 03:30 UTC?
choices: CREATE STREAMING VIEW gold.daily_revenue EVERY DAY AT '03:30 UTC' AS SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM silver.orders GROUP BY order_date
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW gold.daily_revenue SCHEDULE CRON '0 30 3 * * ?' AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM silver.orders GROUP BY order_date
CREATE TABLE gold.daily_revenue SCHEDULE CRON '0 30 3 * * ?' AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM silver.orders GROUP BY order_date
CREATE VIEW gold.daily_revenue REFRESH DAILY AT '03:30' TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM silver.orders GROUP BY order_date
questions.explanation: Materialized views (and streaming tables) take SCHEDULE CRON with Quartz syntax, or SCHEDULE EVERY n HOURS/DAYS. TRIGGER ON UPDATE refreshes them when the sources change.

questions.question: A materialized view is created and refreshed from a Pro SQL warehouse. Which compute does the actual data processing for the refresh, and how is it billed?
choices: The creator's all-purpose cluster, billed at the all-purpose DBU rate
A job cluster in the customer's account, billed at the jobs compute DBU rate
Serverless pipelines, billed as serverless pipeline DBUs
The SQL warehouse does the processing, billed at the warehouse's DBU rate
questions.explanation: Creating and refreshing materialized views and streaming tables runs on serverless pipelines, separate from the SQL warehouse. The warehouse's compute is used only to coordinate the operation.

questions.question: A materialized view must reflect a late correction to its source data right away, without waiting for its schedule. What should the engineer run?
choices: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold.daily_revenue
MSCK REPAIR TABLE gold.daily_revenue
OPTIMIZE gold.daily_revenue
ALTER VIEW gold.daily_revenue RECOMPILE
questions.explanation: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW updates the stored results; it is synchronous by default, and ASYNC returns immediately. Databricks uses a cost model to pick an incremental or a full recompute.

questions.question: In a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines Python file (from pyspark import pipelines as dp), a function decorated with @dp.table returns spark.readStream.table('silver.events'). What is created?
choices: A temporary view that isn't published to Unity Catalog
A materialized view, because @dp.table always creates materialized views
A streaming table, because the function returns a streaming DataFrame
A standard Unity Catalog view
questions.explanation: @dp.table creates a streaming table when the function returns a streaming DataFrame (readStream) and a materialized view when it returns a batch DataFrame. @dp.materialized_view states a materialized view explicitly, and @dp.temporary_view creates a pipeline-scoped view. The legacy module was import dlt.

questions.question: An engineer changes the WHERE clause of an existing streaming table's query to remove a filter. What happens to the rows that the old filter excluded?
choices: The streaming table is dropped and rebuilt on the next refresh
They are added through the _rescued_data column on the next refresh
Nothing; only new data uses the new query unless you run a full refresh
They are reprocessed automatically on the next refresh
questions.explanation: A streaming table refresh processes only rows that are new since the last update, using the current definition. Earlier results are not recomputed. REFRESH STREAMING TABLE ... FULL reprocesses everything, which is risky if the source has short retention (Kafka, for example).

questions.question: A materialized view should refresh automatically whenever its upstream source tables change, rather than on a fixed schedule. Which clause does this?
choices: SCHEDULE EVERY 0 MINUTES
WITH CHANGE DATA FEED
REFRESH ON READ
TRIGGER ON UPDATE
questions.explanation: TRIGGER ON UPDATE refreshes a materialized view or streaming table when its sources are updated, which is the data-driven alternative to SCHEDULE CRON or SCHEDULE EVERY.

questions.question: BI users need a gold object that always shows the current base data, holds no stored copy, and returns results computed when queried. Which object fits?
choices: A materialized view
A standard view (CREATE VIEW)
A streaming table
A managed table built with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT
questions.explanation: A standard view is a saved query evaluated at read time against the current data, with nothing persisted. Materialized views and CTAS tables store results that can go stale between refreshes.

questions.question: A pipeline defines CONSTRAINT valid_email EXPECT (email IS NOT NULL) with no ON VIOLATION clause. What happens to rows with a NULL email?
choices: They are written to the target, and the violations are counted in metrics
The pipeline update fails as soon as the first violating row appears
They are dropped from the target, and the violation is logged
They are moved into a quarantine table that is created automatically
questions.explanation: An expectation with no action uses warn: invalid records are kept and counted in the metrics. ON VIOLATION DROP ROW removes them, and ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE stops the update.

questions.question: Which SQL expectation removes rows with a non-positive amount from a silver streaming table but lets the pipeline keep running?
choices: CONSTRAINT positive_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION IGNORE
CONSTRAINT positive_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
CONSTRAINT positive_amount EXPECT (amount > 0)
questions.explanation: DROP ROW discards the invalid records and records metrics. FAIL UPDATE stops the update, and leaving out the clause keeps the records (warn).

questions.question: A gold table feeds financial reporting. If even one record has a NULL account_id, the update must stop so that nothing is published. Which expectation action does this?
choices: ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
No ON VIOLATION clause, so the default warn applies
ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
ON VIOLATION QUARANTINE
questions.explanation: FAIL UPDATE stops the pipeline update when the expectation is violated, so the transaction is not committed and the cause can be investigated. There is no built-in QUARANTINE action; quarantining is a design pattern.

questions.question: In a Python pipeline file, which decorator drops records that have a NULL id from the dataset being defined?
choices: @dp.expect('valid_id', 'id IS NOT NULL')
@dp.expect_or_fail('valid_id', 'id IS NOT NULL')
@dp.expect_or_drop('valid_id', 'id IS NOT NULL')
@dp.expect_all('valid_id', 'id IS NOT NULL')
questions.explanation: expect keeps records (warn), expect_or_drop removes them, and expect_or_fail stops the update. The expect_all variants take a dict of several named constraints, for example @dp.expect_all_or_drop({'valid_id': 'id IS NOT NULL', 'valid_ts': 'ts IS NOT NULL'}).

questions.question: Where can an engineer see how many records passed or failed each expectation in a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipeline?
choices: Only in the driver's stdout logs on the pipeline's cluster
The pipeline UI's Data quality tab and the pipeline event log
In the _rescued_data column of each target table
In the output of DESCRIBE HISTORY on each target table
questions.explanation: Expectation metrics (for warn and drop actions) are shown in the pipeline UI and recorded in the event log, which can be queried for reporting. Datasets with no expectations have no data quality metrics.

questions.question: An engineer runs ALTER TABLE main.silver.payments ADD CONSTRAINT positive_amount CHECK (amount > 0). Later, an INSERT includes one row with amount = -5. What happens?
choices: The constraint is dropped automatically so that the write can succeed
Only the row with amount = -5 is skipped, and the other rows are written
The whole INSERT fails, and none of its rows are written
The row is written, and a warning is added to the table history
questions.explanation: Delta CHECK and NOT NULL constraints are enforced: any violation fails the whole transaction. Adding a constraint also fails if existing rows already violate it.

questions.question: A silver table has a PRIMARY KEY (order_id) constraint, and a load inserts two rows with the same order_id. What happens?
choices: The second row is dropped automatically to keep the key unique
The insert succeeds, because primary key constraints aren't enforced
The two rows are merged into one row automatically
The insert fails, because primary keys are enforced like CHECK constraints
questions.explanation: Primary key, foreign key, and unique constraints on Databricks are informational: they document relationships and can help the optimizer, but they don't block duplicates. Enforce uniqueness with deduplication logic or expectations.

questions.question: Invalid records must not reach the silver table, but they must be kept for investigation instead of being discarded. What is the recommended pipeline pattern?
choices: Use the warn action so that invalid rows land in silver alongside the valid ones
Turn off all expectations and fix the data later in the gold layer instead
Use ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE so that the invalid rows stay in the source system
Drop invalid rows from silver, and write them to a quarantine table using the inverted rules
questions.explanation: Quarantining keeps silver clean (with expect_or_drop or DROP ROW) while a second dataset filtered on the negated conditions captures the bad records for review and reprocessing.

questions.question: A task has a 30-minute timeout and a retry policy of 2 retries. How do the timeout and the retries interact?
choices: The timeout applies to each attempt, so every retry gets 30 minutes
Retries are turned off whenever a timeout is set
Only the final retry is subject to the timeout
The 30 minutes is shared by the original attempt and both retries
questions.explanation: In Lakeflow Jobs, when both Timeout and Retries are set, the timeout applies to each retry. The retry policy also sets the retry interval and whether a timed-out attempt should be retried.

questions.question: A cleanup task should run after its upstream tasks finish, whether they succeeded or failed. Which Run if condition should it use?
choices: All done
None failed
All succeeded
At least one succeeded
questions.explanation: All done runs the task once every dependency has run, regardless of how they finished, which is ideal for cleanup or for releasing resources.

questions.question: A notification task should run only if at least one of its upstream ingestion tasks failed. Which Run if condition should it use?
choices: All failed
All done
At least one succeeded
At least one failed
questions.explanation: At least one failed runs the task when any dependency has failed. If the condition isn't met (everything succeeded), the task is marked Excluded instead of failing.

questions.question: What is the default Run if condition for a task that has dependencies?
choices: At least one succeeded
All succeeded
None failed
All done
questions.explanation: By default a task runs only when all of its dependencies have run and succeeded. When the condition isn't met, the task is marked Upstream failed.

questions.question: Which Run if condition means that none of the dependencies failed and at least one dependency ran?
choices: All done
None failed
All succeeded
At least one succeeded
questions.explanation: There are six conditions: All succeeded (the default), At least one succeeded, None failed, All done, At least one failed, and All failed. Upstream tasks marked Excluded count as successful when the conditions are evaluated.

questions.question: A validation notebook task named validate sets a task value row_count. The load task should run only when row_count is greater than 0. How should the job be built?
choices: Give load the Run if condition All succeeded, which checks row_count automatically
An If/else task testing {{tasks.validate.values.row_count}} > 0, with load on the true branch
Add a For each task that loops over row_count with a concurrency of 0
Have the validate task raise an exception so that load is skipped
questions.explanation: An If/else condition task compares operands, which can be task values, job parameters, or other dynamic value references. Downstream tasks depend on its (true) or (false) outcome. The condition task runs no code and needs no compute.

questions.question: An If/else condition task compares the task value 12.0 with 12. Which statement about the result is correct?
choices: Both comparisons are false, because every operator compares values as strings
Both comparisons fail, because task values must be integers
12.0 == 12 is true, because every operator compares values numerically
12.0 == 12 is false (string comparison); 12.0 >= 12 is true (numeric)
questions.explanation: In If/else tasks, == and != compare strings, while >, >=, <, and <= compare numbers. Mixing up the two is a common source of unexpected branch outcomes.

questions.question: One ingestion notebook must run once for each region in the list ["us", "eu", "apac"]. Which Lakeflow Jobs feature does this, and how does the notebook receive the current region?
choices: A For each task over the list, with the region passed as {{input}}
Three copies of the notebook task, joined by Run if dependencies
A job with a continuous trigger that rotates through the regions
An If/else condition task with a branch for each region
questions.explanation: For each loops over a JSON array (or a task value or job parameter reference) and runs its nested task once per element. {{input}} (or {{input.<key>}} for objects) passes the item, for example as a notebook parameter.

questions.question: A For each task over 40 table names runs its iterations one after another, which takes too long. What should be changed?
choices: Raise the For each task's Concurrency (default 1)
Raise the job's maximum concurrent runs to 40
Change the job to use a continuous trigger
Add 40 retries to the nested notebook task
questions.explanation: For each runs iterations one at a time by default (Concurrency = 1). Raising Concurrency runs several iterations in parallel. The job-level maximum concurrent runs applies to whole job runs, not to iterations.

questions.question: Which statement about the For each task is true?
choices: It always runs all iterations in parallel, with no limit
Its nested task must be a SQL task
Its nested task can't be another For each task
It can only loop over integers produced by a range() expression
questions.explanation: For each runs one nested task (notebook, SQL, Run Job, and so on) per input. Nesting a For each directly inside a For each isn't allowed; a Run Job task that calls a job with its own loop is one workaround.

questions.question: In a 10-task job run, task 6 fails, and tasks 7 and 8 depend on it. After the bug is fixed, what does Repair run do?
choices: It creates a new job that contains only the failed tasks
It re-runs only task 6 and marks tasks 7 and 8 as succeeded
It re-runs only task 6 and its dependents, tasks 7 and 8
It re-runs all 10 tasks from the beginning
questions.explanation: Repair run saves time and compute by skipping tasks that already succeeded. The repair dialog also lets you change parameters for the tasks being repaired. It applies to jobs with two or more tasks; a single-task job is re-run with Run now.

questions.question: A task appended half of its output to a table and then failed. What risk should the engineer consider before repairing the run?
choices: Repair isn't allowed when a task has written partial output
The task restarts from the beginning, so it may write duplicate data
Repair rolls back the table's partial writes automatically before re-running
Repair resumes the task from the last committed micro-batch, so nothing is duplicated
questions.explanation: Lakeflow Jobs doesn't make tasks idempotent. Design tasks for safe re-runs, for example with MERGE, overwriting a partition, COPY INTO's file tracking, or streaming checkpoints.

questions.question: Several pipelines need to start the same shared 'refresh dimensions' job as one step of their own workflows. Which task type supports this modular design?
choices: A Dashboard task that refreshes the dimensions
An If/else condition task that points to the other job's ID
A copy of each of the shared job's notebooks pasted into every pipeline
A Run Job task that triggers the existing job
questions.explanation: The Run Job task triggers another Lakeflow job as a task, so the parent can orchestrate reusable child jobs. The parent waits for the child to finish and gets its outcome.

questions.question: A task in a production job should be skipped temporarily, but its configuration and history must be kept. What should the engineer do?
choices: Delete the task and recreate it later from memory
Set the task's timeout to 0 seconds so it ends at once
Disable the task, which skips it but keeps it in the job
Set the task's retries to 0 so it never runs again
questions.explanation: Disabling a task keeps its configuration and run history. Downstream tasks still evaluate their Run if conditions, and the disabled task shows the Disabled status.

questions.question: Which compute must a SQL task in Lakeflow Jobs use?
choices: Any job cluster that runs Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS or above
A serverless or Pro SQL warehouse
A classic SQL warehouse only
An all-purpose cluster in dedicated access mode
questions.explanation: SQL tasks (query, alert, or SQL file) need Databricks SQL with a serverless or Pro SQL warehouse. Dashboard tasks have the same requirement.

questions.question: A job has to run etl/silver/build_orders.sql from the team's Git repository; the file holds several statements separated by semicolons. How should the task be configured?
choices: A Pipeline task with the .sql file pasted into its configuration
A notebook task that points at the .sql file, using an all-purpose cluster
A SQL task of type File, pointing at the file in the Git repository
A Dashboard task that runs the .sql file as one of its datasets
questions.explanation: The SQL task's File option runs a .sql file stored in the workspace (Git folders included) or in a remote Git repository. Git paths are relative, without a leading / or ./, and one job can use only one remote repository.

questions.question: After the nightly ETL finishes, a published AI/BI dashboard must be refreshed and its subscribers emailed. Which task does this, and what does it require?
choices: A Dashboard task, using a serverless or Pro SQL warehouse
A SQL Alert task with the dashboard ID passed as a parameter
A notebook task that calls display() on every dashboard dataset
A Pipeline task that has the dashboard as its target
questions.explanation: The Dashboard task refreshes a published dashboard and can email subscribers or notification destinations. The configurer needs at least CAN VIEW on the dashboard, and a dashboard filter whose URL identifier matches a job parameter key takes that parameter's value.

questions.question: A Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipeline has to run as one step of a multi-task job, and occasionally be reprocessed completely. Which task type is used, and which option reprocesses everything?
choices: A SQL task that runs REFRESH PIPELINE ALL
A Run Job task with its retries set to 0
A Pipeline task, with its Full refresh option enabled
A notebook task that imports the pipeline's source files
questions.explanation: The Pipeline task starts an update of an existing pipeline, which keeps its own compute and source settings. Full refresh can be selected when the task is configured, to rebuild the pipeline's tables.

questions.question: A job containing a Pipeline task is set to a maximum of 5 concurrent runs, yet only one run is ever active at a time. Why?
choices: A pipeline runs only one update at a time, which caps the job at one run
Pipeline tasks always use a job cluster that can't be shared
The workspace limits every job to a single concurrent run
Concurrent runs are only allowed with a continuous trigger type
questions.explanation: A pipeline runs one update at a time, so Lakeflow Jobs caps a job containing a Pipeline task at one concurrent run, whatever max_concurrent_runs says.

questions.question: A notebook task is configured with the parameter run_date. How does the notebook code read its value?
choices: dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get('run_date')
dbutils.widgets.get('run_date')
os.environ['run_date']
spark.conf.get('run_date')
questions.explanation: Notebook task parameters are passed as widget values and read with dbutils.widgets.get. Task values are a different mechanism, for passing data between tasks.

questions.question: A job defines the job-level parameter env with the default 'dev'. How can a task's settings refer to that value?
choices: ${var.env}
{{parameters.env}}
{{job.env.value}}
{{job.parameters.env}}
questions.explanation: Dynamic value references use double curly braces, for example {{job.parameters.<name>}}, {{job.run_id}}, or {{tasks.<task>.values.<key>}}. ${var.env} is bundle variable syntax, which is resolved at deploy time rather than at run time.

questions.question: A Python notebook task named extract has to pass the number of rows it loaded to later tasks. Which code sets the value?
choices: dbutils.widgets.set('row_count', row_count)
dbutils.notebook.exit(row_count) on its own, which every downstream task can read
spark.conf.set('tasks.extract.row_count', row_count)
dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key='row_count', value=row_count)
questions.explanation: Task values are set with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set and read later with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey='extract', key='row_count', default=..., debugValue=...) or with {{tasks.extract.values.row_count}}.

questions.question: Which statement about task values is correct?
choices: Values are limited to 10 characters and must be strings
Values must be JSON-serializable and at most 48 KiB
Values persist across job runs and can be read by later runs
Values can be any Python object, including open Spark DataFrames
questions.explanation: Task values are for small metadata, such as counts, flags, or lists of table names. For large data, write to a table or a volume and pass a reference to it instead.

questions.question: Task A ingests data. Tasks B and C each depend on A, and task D depends on both B and C. With default settings, when does D start?
choices: Only after the whole job finishes, as a separate run
As soon as either B or C succeeds
After both B and C have completed successfully
At the same moment as A, because the tasks are in the same job
questions.explanation: Lakeflow Jobs runs tasks as a DAG. B and C can run in parallel once A succeeds (fan-out), and D waits for both (fan-in), because the default Run if condition is All succeeded.

questions.question: Five notebook tasks in one job each create their own job cluster, and startup time dominates the run. With classic compute, what reduces this overhead?
choices: Give each task a larger single-node cluster
Turn the job into five separate jobs with their own schedules
Raise the job's maximum concurrent runs to 5
Have the tasks share one job cluster defined at the job level
questions.explanation: A shared job cluster is created once for the run and reused by several tasks, which avoids repeated startup and still uses cheaper jobs compute. Serverless jobs compute is another way to cut startup overhead.

questions.question: A task parameter should hold the date of the run in ISO format (for example 2026-10-07), without any code computing it. Which value should be used?
choices: ${bundle.run_date}
{{current_date()}}
{{job.parameters.today}}, which is filled in automatically
{{job.start_time.iso_date}}
questions.explanation: Dynamic value references provide run metadata such as job.start_time.<format>, job.run_id, job.trigger.type, and job.trigger.file_arrival.location. Expressions inside the braces are not evaluated, so function calls don't work.

questions.question: The team ships its transformation logic as a Python package. Which task type runs a function from it through an entry point defined in the package?
choices: A Dashboard task
A Python wheel task
A SQL Alert task
An If/else condition task
questions.explanation: A Python wheel task installs the .whl and calls the named entry point, passing it parameters (and job parameters as keyword arguments). It is common when code is packaged and deployed with bundles.

questions.question: Which storage locations can a Lakeflow Jobs file arrival trigger monitor?
choices: A folder on the workspace user's laptop
Only the legacy DBFS root (dbfs:/FileStore)
Any public HTTP or FTP URL that the job can reach
A Unity Catalog volume or external location
questions.explanation: File arrival triggers require Unity Catalog. They watch a volume or an external location, and need READ permission on the location and CAN MANAGE on the job. Enabling file events on the external location is recommended.

questions.question: How often does a file arrival trigger check for new files, and what does checking cost?
choices: About every minute (best effort), with only cloud listing costs
It checks only when someone opens the job page in the UI
It checks continuously in real time, and each check uses serverless DBUs
It checks once an hour, and each check is billed as a job run
questions.explanation: The trigger tries to check for new files every minute (depending on storage performance). It doesn't add Databricks charges, only the cloud provider's costs for listing.

questions.question: Without file events enabled on the external location, which limits apply to file arrival triggers?
choices: Only one job per workspace can use a trigger, with up to 1 million files
At most 5 jobs per workspace can use a trigger, and there is no limit on files
At most 50 such jobs per workspace, and up to 10,000 files per location
There is no limit on jobs, but each location can hold at most 100 files
questions.explanation: Without file events, the limits are 50 file-arrival-triggered jobs per workspace and 10,000 files per monitored location. With file events enabled, there is no file count limit, which is why file events are recommended.

questions.question: An upstream system overwrites daily_extract.csv in a monitored volume each day, using the same file name. The file arrival trigger never fires. Why?
choices: File arrival triggers ignore CSV files and accept only Parquet
The volume must be converted to a Delta table first
Overwriting an existing file name doesn't count as a new file
The trigger fires only when files are deleted from the volume
questions.explanation: File arrival triggers react to newly arriving files. Have the producer write uniquely named files (for example with a timestamp in the name) so that each delivery triggers a run.

questions.question: Files for a batch arrive one by one over several minutes, and the job should start only once the batch has finished landing. Which file arrival setting helps?
choices: Wait after last change
Minimum time between triggers set to 0
Maximum concurrent runs set to 10
A retry policy with 3 retries
questions.explanation: Wait after last change debounces the trigger: the run starts only once the location has been quiet for the configured number of seconds. Minimum time between triggers is a cooldown between runs.

questions.question: Files arrive constantly, but the job should run at most once every 15 minutes. Which setting enforces that?
choices: A job-level timeout of 15 minutes
Minimum time between triggers (900 seconds)
A For each concurrency setting of 15
Wait after last change (900 seconds)
questions.explanation: Minimum time between triggers limits the job to one run per interval, a cooldown. Wait after last change waits for a quiet period, which might never come while files keep arriving.

questions.question: A job should start when either of two upstream Unity Catalog tables is updated. What does a table update trigger support?
choices: Exactly one table per trigger, which must be an external table
Up to 10 tables per trigger, firing when any or all are updated
Only views, because tables can't be monitored
Unlimited tables, but only the all-tables-updated condition
questions.explanation: Table update triggers monitor Unity Catalog managed and Delta tables, materialized views, streaming tables, and views or metric views that depend on supported tables (each view's sources count toward the limit of 10). The condition can be Any table is updated or All tables are updated.

questions.question: A table update trigger has been configured, but the job never starts when the monitored table changes. Which permission problem is the most likely cause?
choices: The job owner lacks MODIFY on the monitored table
The monitored table must be shared publicly through Delta Sharing
The trigger needs workspace admin rights to watch any table
The job's Run as principal lacks SELECT on the monitored table
questions.explanation: The Run as principal must have SELECT on every object the table update trigger monitors.

questions.question: A job uses the Quartz cron expression 0 0 2 * * ? with the time zone set to UTC. When does it run?
choices: Every Monday and Tuesday at 00:00 UTC
On the 2nd day of every month at midnight
Every 2 minutes
Every day at 02:00 UTC
questions.explanation: Quartz cron fields are second, minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week (with an optional year). 0 0 2 * * ? means second 0, minute 0, hour 2, every day; ? means no specific day of the week.

questions.question: Which statement about scheduled triggers in Lakeflow Jobs is correct?
choices: Runs can be delayed by minutes, and must be at least 10 seconds apart
Scheduled runs are guaranteed to start exactly on the second
Schedules are written in standard five-field Unix cron only
A schedule can run a job at most once an hour, for any job
questions.explanation: Schedules can be simple (every N units) or advanced (with Quartz cron syntax, start time, and time zone). Databricks enforces at least 10 seconds between runs, and infrastructure issues can delay runs, so very low latency calls for streaming or continuous jobs.

questions.question: An hourly job scheduled in a time zone that observes daylight saving time sometimes appears skipped or delayed when the clocks change. What does Databricks recommend for running on every absolute hour?
choices: Set the schedule's time zone to UTC
Use a file arrival trigger instead
Use a simple schedule of every 59 minutes
Set the maximum concurrent runs to 2
questions.explanation: In time zones with daylight saving time, an hourly schedule can skip or shift a run when DST begins or ends. UTC has no DST, so the runs fall on every absolute hour.

questions.question: What does a continuous trigger do in Lakeflow Jobs?
choices: It runs the job every 10 seconds on a fixed schedule, even if the previous run is still going
It starts a run for every new file, with no debouncing
It starts a new run whenever the previous run completes or fails
It runs the job once, and then keeps the cluster up indefinitely
questions.explanation: Continuous jobs restart automatically (failures use exponential backoff), which suits streaming workloads. A continuous trigger excludes scheduled, file arrival, and table update triggers on the same job.

questions.question: A vendor drops files into a volume at unpredictable times, sometimes twice a day and sometimes not for three days. Processing should start soon after each delivery without wasting runs. Which trigger fits?
choices: A file arrival trigger on the volume
A continuous trigger
A manual trigger whenever someone notices the files
A schedule that runs every 5 minutes
questions.explanation: Data-driven triggers start work when data actually arrives. A polling schedule would waste runs and add latency, and a continuous job would keep compute busy waiting for rare files.

questions.question: Another team's job refreshes the Unity Catalog table finance.silver.ledger at varying times. Your gold job should run right after each refresh, without coordinating schedules between the teams. Which trigger fits?
choices: A file arrival trigger on the other team's notebook folder
A Run Job task inside the other team's job, which you don't own
A table update trigger on finance.silver.ledger
A schedule set an hour after the other team's usual finish time
questions.explanation: A table update trigger reacts to commits on the table itself, so it follows the data whatever schedule the producer keeps. Guessing at a schedule risks running too early (stale data) or too late.

questions.question: Executives need a summary report refreshed by 07:00 every business day, whether or not new data has arrived. Which trigger fits?
choices: A scheduled trigger for 06:30 on weekdays
A file arrival trigger on the report output folder
A table update trigger on the report table itself
A continuous trigger that refreshes all day
questions.explanation: When the requirement is tied to the calendar or a deadline rather than to data arriving, a time-based schedule is the right choice.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of data-driven triggers (file arrival, table update) over a frequent polling schedule?
choices: Data-driven triggers ignore a job's concurrency settings
Data-driven triggers work without Unity Catalog being enabled
Runs happen only when new data exists, cutting wasted runs
Data-driven triggers guarantee sub-second latency for every run
questions.explanation: A polling schedule that runs every few minutes spends compute even when nothing has changed. Data-driven triggers tie runs to data availability, and their debounce and cooldown settings control how often runs happen.

questions.question: In one job, the transform task should run as soon as the ingest task finishes. Which mechanism should the engineer use?
choices: A schedule on the transform task set 10 minutes after the ingest task
A task dependency in the job's DAG (transform depends on ingest)
A file arrival trigger on the ingest task's output folder
A separate job for transform with a table update trigger
questions.explanation: Triggers start whole jobs; within a job, ordering is expressed with task dependencies. Triggers are for coordinating across independent jobs or with external data arrival.

questions.question: A gold job joins orders and payments, and should run only once both silver tables have been refreshed since its last run. How should the trigger be configured?
choices: A table update trigger on both tables with the condition Any table is updated
A file arrival trigger on the orders table's storage path
Two scheduled triggers, one for each table's usual refresh time
A table update trigger on both tables with the condition All tables are updated
questions.explanation: When several tables are monitored, the trigger can wait until all of them have been updated, which keeps the gold join from running on half-refreshed inputs.

questions.question: A fraud model needs events processed within seconds of arrival. Which design fits best?
choices: A table update trigger with wait after last change set to 60 seconds
A schedule running every 10 seconds, the minimum interval
A streaming workload run as a continuous job (or a continuous pipeline)
A file arrival trigger, which checks for new files roughly every minute
questions.explanation: File arrival checks happen about once a minute and the scheduler isn't meant for low latency. Seconds-level latency calls for a continuously running streaming workload.

questions.question: Month-end close processing must run at 23:00 on the last day of each month. Which trigger fits?
choices: A continuous trigger that checks the date on every run
A scheduled trigger with a last-day-of-month cron expression
A table update trigger on the general ledger table
A file arrival trigger on the finance landing folder
questions.explanation: Calendar-based business processes call for time-based schedules. Quartz cron supports this directly, for example 0 0 23 L * ? where L means the last day of the month.

questions.question: A job started by a file arrival trigger needs to pass the monitored storage location to its notebook as a parameter. Which dynamic value reference provides it?
choices: {{job.parameters.location}}, which is filled in automatically
{{task.notebook_path}}
{{job.trigger.type}}
{{job.trigger.file_arrival.location}}
questions.explanation: Dynamic value references expose trigger metadata: job.trigger.type gives the kind of trigger, and job.trigger.file_arrival.location gives the monitored location for file arrival triggers.

questions.question: A developer wants to start a feature branch from main inside a Databricks Git folder. What do they do?
choices: Ask a workspace admin to create the branch in the Admin settings
Right-click the folder and choose Duplicate, then rename the copy
In the Git dialog, click Create Branch and choose main as the base
Run git checkout -b in a notebook cell attached to any cluster
questions.explanation: The Git folder dialog (opened from the branch button next to a notebook's name, or with Git beside the folder) handles creating, switching, pulling, committing and pushing, merging, rebasing, and resetting.

questions.question: How are changes committed from a Databricks Git folder in the workspace UI?
choices: Save the notebook; every save is committed automatically to main
Enter a commit message and click Commit & Push, a single action
Export the notebook as a .dbc file and upload it to the Git provider
Commit locally first; changes are pushed automatically every night
questions.explanation: In the Git folders UI, committing and pushing is one step. Staging several local commits before pushing requires Git CLI access, which is in Public Preview.

questions.question: A developer has pushed a feature branch from a Git folder and wants it reviewed and merged into main, which is protected. How is the pull request created?
choices: Run databricks bundle deploy, which opens and merges the pull request
Email the notebook to the reviewer, who imports it into main
In the Git provider, such as GitHub, where it is reviewed and merged
Click Merge in the Git folder dialog, which approves the pull request automatically
questions.explanation: Pull requests are a Git provider feature. Databricks docs say that if you can't commit to the default branch, you should create a branch and use your Git provider's interface to open a pull request and merge it.

questions.question: A developer has uncommitted edits on feature-a and switches the Git folder to feature-b. What happens to the edits?
choices: They are discarded automatically when the branch switches
They are stashed and come back only when switching back to feature-a
They carry over to feature-b, as long as they don't conflict
They are committed automatically to feature-a before the switch
questions.explanation: Uncommitted changes follow you to the new branch if they don't conflict. Discard them first if you don't want that. Switching can also remove workspace assets that don't exist on the target branch.

questions.question: A developer clicks Pull in a Git folder while notebooks in it are attached and have run cells. What side effect should they expect?
choices: The notebook outputs are committed to the remote before pulling
The attached cluster restarts and reinstalls all of its libraries
The pull is blocked until every notebook is detached from compute
The notebook state is cleared, as with any pull of upstream changes
questions.explanation: Pulls (and other operations that bring in upstream changes) update the files and clear notebook state. Any conflicts are resolved in the Git folder's conflict UI.

questions.question: Five engineers are working on the same repository. What is the recommended Git folder setup?
choices: Each engineer clones their own Git folder and works on their own branch
Each engineer works on main directly, to avoid merge conflicts
One engineer does every commit for the others from a shared folder
Everyone shares one Git folder so that all changes are visible immediately
questions.explanation: A Git folder has a single checked-out branch. If several people perform Git operations on one folder, one of them can switch the branch for everyone. Each person should have their own folder and branch.

questions.question: Which statement about rebase and reset in Databricks Git folders is correct?
choices: Rebase and reset both create a new merge commit and never force-push
Rebase is the recommended default because it never rewrites history
Reset affects only the local copy and never changes the remote branch
Both rewrite history and force-push, so merge is recommended for beginners
questions.explanation: After a rebase, Git folders run git push --force. Reset is git reset --hard followed by git push --force, and it loses changes on both the local and remote branch. Merge doesn't rewrite history.

questions.question: A team uses a shared production Git folder as the code source for its jobs. How should that folder be kept up to date?
choices: By any developer pulling into it manually whenever they remember
By copying notebooks into it from personal folders through the UI
By developers committing directly from the production folder
Only by automation, such as CI/CD calling the Repos API on merge
questions.explanation: Production Git folders live outside /Workspace/Users and should be updated only by automation, and jobs run as service principals with limited permissions. For full CI/CD, Databricks recommends Declarative Automation Bundles.

questions.question: In a bundle's databricks.yml, a custom variable catalog is declared with the default dev_catalog. How is it referenced elsewhere in the configuration?
choices: ${variables.catalog.default}
${var.catalog}
{{var.catalog}}
$catalog
questions.explanation: Custom variables are declared under the top-level variables mapping and referenced as ${var.<name>}. Double curly braces are Lakeflow Jobs dynamic value references, which are resolved at run time instead.

questions.question: A bundle variable has a value in several places. Which list orders them from highest to lowest precedence?
choices: The default, the target's variables mapping, variable-overrides.json, BUNDLE_VAR_<name>, then the --var CLI flag
BUNDLE_VAR_<name>, the default, the --var CLI flag, variable-overrides.json, then the target's variables mapping
The target's variables mapping, the --var CLI flag, the default, variable-overrides.json, then BUNDLE_VAR_<name>
The --var CLI flag, BUNDLE_VAR_<name>, variable-overrides.json, the target's variables mapping, then the default
questions.explanation: The CLI uses the first value it finds, in this order: --var, then BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variables, then variable-overrides.json, then target-level values, then the declared default.

questions.question: A CI/CD pipeline must set the bundle variable warehouse_id without editing databricks.yml and without passing command-line flags. How can it do this?
choices: Add warehouse_id to the profile in ~/.databrickscfg
Set the environment variable BUNDLE_VAR_warehouse_id
Set the environment variable VAR_warehouse_id
Set the environment variable DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID
questions.explanation: Any custom variable can be supplied through an environment variable named BUNDLE_VAR_<variable_name>, which is convenient in CI systems where secrets and settings arrive as environment variables.

questions.question: The variable catalog should be dev_catalog by default but prod_catalog when deploying to the prod target. How is this written in databricks.yml?
choices: Declare two variables, catalog_dev and catalog_prod, and choose between them with an if statement in the YAML
Declare the variable with default dev_catalog, and under targets: prod: add variables: catalog: prod_catalog
Set catalog in the bundle mapping, which every target ignores
Declare the variable separately inside each job's task definition
questions.explanation: Targets override top-level settings. A target-level variables mapping supplies environment-specific values, so the same resource definitions can be promoted across dev, test, and prod.

questions.question: A job in a bundle needs the ID of the SQL warehouse named 'Shared Analytics', and that ID differs in each workspace. Which feature avoids hardcoding the IDs?
choices: A lookup variable that resolves the warehouse ID by its name
A complex variable that contains the warehouse's full JSON definition
A BUNDLE_VAR_lookup environment variable set in CI
The ${workspace.current_user.userName} substitution
questions.explanation: Lookup variables resolve the IDs of named objects (alerts, cluster policies, clusters, dashboards, instance pools, jobs, metastores, pipelines, queries, service principals, warehouses) in whichever workspace the target deploys to.

questions.question: A team wants one bundle variable to hold an entire cluster specification (node type, worker count, Spark version) that several jobs can reuse. How is it declared?
choices: As a plain string holding comma-separated cluster settings
A complex variable (type: complex) holding the cluster definition
As a BUNDLE_VAR_ environment variable containing YAML
As a lookup variable that points to a cluster policy
questions.explanation: type: complex (the only allowed type value) lets a variable hold a structured object rather than a single scalar value, so a configuration block can be reused through ${var.<name>}.

questions.question: Pipelines should write to a schema named after the deployment target, such as sales_dev or sales_prod, without a separate variable for each target. Which substitution helps?
choices: sales_${workspace.target_name}
sales_${bundle.target}
sales_{{job.target}}
sales_${var.target}, which is predefined
questions.explanation: Substitutions such as ${bundle.target}, ${bundle.name}, ${workspace.current_user.userName}, ${workspace.root_path}, and ${resources.jobs.<key>.id} are filled in from the deployment context.

questions.question: The top-level resources mapping defines a job with a notebook task and a small job cluster. The prod target needs a bigger cluster but the same task. What is the right approach?
choices: Override only the cluster settings under targets: prod:; they merge with the top-level job
Copy the complete job definition into the prod target, because targets replace resources entirely
Create a second bundle for production with its own copy of the job
Change the cluster size by hand in the workspace after each deployment
questions.explanation: Target-level resource settings are merged with the top-level resources mapping, overriding only what the target specifies. This keeps one codebase, with environment-specific overrides.

questions.question: A developer deploys a bundle to a target with mode: development. Which behaviors does that mode turn on?
choices: Resources are deployed with no prefix, and every schedule starts running immediately
Every job is forced to run as a service principal identity
Deployment fails unless the current Git branch matches the target's branch
A [dev <user>] name prefix, paused schedules, and development pipelines
questions.explanation: Development mode is built for safe iteration: per-user prefixes avoid name collisions, paused schedules keep dev jobs from running unattended, development pipelines are used, concurrent runs are allowed, and the deployment lock is turned off. Presets can fine-tune each of these behaviors.

questions.question: Which checks does mode: production add to a bundle target?
choices: It skips validation entirely so that production deployments are faster
It deploys only the notebooks and leaves out the jobs and pipelines
It adds a [prod] prefix to every resource name and pauses all of the schedules
It checks the Git branch, requires non-development pipelines, and blocks cluster overrides
questions.explanation: Production mode guards against accidental deployments: the branch check can be bypassed with --force, --cluster-id overrides are rejected, and Databricks recommends a service principal through run_as.

questions.question: What do Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles) package and deploy?
choices: Only cluster definitions, which are stored as JSON in Unity Catalog
Only notebook files, copied into a shared workspace folder
Source code plus YAML definitions of resources such as jobs and pipelines
Docker images of the Databricks Runtime, pushed to a container registry
questions.explanation: A bundle is infrastructure-as-code: databricks.yml (plus any included files) describes resources (jobs, pipelines, dashboards, and more), variables, and targets. The bundle is versioned in Git and deployed with the Databricks CLI. The March 2026 rename was fully backward compatible.

questions.question: A team wants to start a new bundle project from a standard Python project layout with example jobs and pipelines. Which command should it run?
choices: databricks bundle init
databricks repos create --bundle
databricks workspace import-dir --template
databricks bundle deploy --new
questions.explanation: bundle init creates a new bundle from a built-in template (such as default-python) or a custom one, giving a databricks.yml, resource files, and source code that can then be validated and deployed.

questions.question: A bundle's databricks.yml is becoming too long. How can each job and pipeline definition live in its own YAML file under resources/?
choices: Use the top-level include mapping, for example include: - resources/*.yml
Use separate bundles for each file and deploy them all with one --all flag
Use the import keyword inside every job definition
Use the sync mapping, which merges every YAML file automatically
questions.explanation: include lists additional configuration files (globs are allowed) that are merged into the bundle configuration. sync controls which source files are uploaded to the workspace.

questions.question: Using bundles, how does a team promote the same pipeline code from dev to test to prod?
choices: Point the prod jobs at the developers' personal Git folders
Export the dev jobs as JSON and import them into prod by hand
Define dev, test, and prod targets, and deploy the same bundle to each with -t
Keep three copies of the code, one for each environment, in separate repositories
questions.explanation: The same versioned bundle is deployed to each target. Targets supply environment-specific hosts, variables, modes, and overrides, so the code stays the same while the configuration varies.

questions.question: Production jobs deployed by a bundle should not run under any individual engineer's identity. What should the prod target configure?
choices: mode: development, so that the jobs run as the user who deployed them
permissions with CAN VIEW granted to all users
run_as set to a service principal
A personal access token for the team lead, saved in databricks.yml
questions.explanation: run_as sets the identity the bundle's jobs and pipelines run as (user_name or service_principal_name). A service principal means production doesn't depend on one person's account or permissions, and it is the recommended identity in production mode. CI/CD should also deploy as a service principal.

questions.question: Which CLI command checks that a bundle's configuration files are syntactically correct, and shows the resolved values, before anything is deployed?
choices: databricks bundle lint
databricks bundle deploy --dry-run
databricks bundle validate
databricks bundle summary --check
questions.explanation: bundle validate checks the configuration and warns about properties that aren't in the resource schemas. Running it with --output json shows the resolved variables and substitutions. CI pipelines usually run it before deploying.

questions.question: Which command deploys a bundle to the prod target that is defined in databricks.yml?
choices: databricks bundle deploy -t prod
databricks deploy bundle --env prod
databricks bundle run --target prod --deploy
databricks jobs create --bundle prod
questions.explanation: bundle deploy uploads the files and creates or updates the defined resources in the target workspace. -t (--target) selects the target; without it, the target marked default: true is used.

questions.question: A bundle defines a job under the resource key nightly_etl. After deploying to dev, how does the developer run it from the CLI?
choices: databricks bundle run -t dev nightly_etl
databricks run job nightly_etl
databricks bundle deploy -t dev --run
databricks jobs run-now nightly_etl --bundle
questions.explanation: bundle run starts a job, pipeline, app, or script defined in the bundle, identified by its resource key, in the chosen target.

questions.question: A feature is cancelled, and every job, pipeline, and file that its bundle deployed to the dev workspace should be removed. Which command does this?
choices: databricks bundle deploy -t dev --empty
databricks bundle destroy -t dev
databricks workspace delete --recursive /
databricks bundle validate --remove
questions.explanation: bundle destroy deletes the jobs, pipelines, other resources, and artifacts that were previously deployed for the target. It asks for confirmation unless --auto-approve is passed.

questions.question: Before a production deployment, a reviewer wants to see which resources would be created, updated, or deleted, without changing anything. Which command shows that?
choices: databricks bundle plan -t prod
databricks bundle run -t prod --dry
databricks bundle destroy -t prod --preview
databricks bundle init -t prod
questions.explanation: bundle plan shows the deployment plan for the current configuration, much like a Terraform plan, so changes can be reviewed before databricks bundle deploy applies them.

questions.question: A job was built by hand in the UI, and the team now wants to manage it with a bundle without creating a duplicate. Which commands should it use?
choices: databricks bundle destroy, then recreate the job by hand from the UI
bundle generate job --existing-job-id <id>, then bundle deployment bind
databricks bundle init --from-job <id>, then delete the original job
databricks jobs export <id> > job.json, then rename the file databricks.yml
questions.explanation: bundle generate writes configuration for existing jobs, pipelines, dashboards, and similar resources. bundle deployment bind links a bundle resource to its existing workspace counterpart, so the next deploy updates that object instead of creating a new one.

questions.question: A GitHub Actions workflow runs databricks bundle deploy against production. How should it authenticate?
choices: With the workspace admin's username and password, set as environment variables
With a developer's personal access token, stored in the repository's README
With interactive OAuth user-to-machine login, run by hand on each deploy
As a service principal, using OAuth M2M or workload identity federation
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends service principals for CI/CD. OAuth M2M (DATABRICKS_HOST, DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID, DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET) is the standard automated auth for the CLI, and workload identity federation (OIDC token federation) removes long-lived secrets altogether. PATs and personal accounts are discouraged for automation.

questions.question: In a job's matrix view of run history, what does the height of each run bar and task bar represent?
choices: The number of retries it took
The duration of that run or task run
The amount of data the task processed
The number of executors it used
questions.explanation: The matrix view shows a job's runs side by side, task by task. Bar height shows duration, and color shows status: green succeeded, red failed, pink skipped, yellow waiting for retry, and grey pending, canceled, or timed out.

questions.question: A nightly job that used to take 40 minutes now takes 70. The engineer wants to find which task is responsible and when the slowdown began. What is the quickest way?
choices: Open a single run's notebook output and read through the print statements
Restart the cluster and see whether the next run is faster
Check the workspace audit log for the job's creation date
Compare each task's bar heights across recent runs in the matrix view
questions.explanation: The matrix view lines up each task's duration across runs, so a regression in one task stands out against its historical baseline. You can then drill into that task's run, and its Spark UI or query profile.

questions.question: Leadership wants job duration trends over the past 6 months, but the Jobs UI only reaches back about two months. Where should the engineer look?
choices: DESCRIBE HISTORY on the job's output table, which records task durations
The cluster's driver logs, which keep every run since the cluster was created
The notebook revision history of the job's main notebook
The system.lakeflow system tables, such as job_run_timeline
questions.explanation: The Jobs UI keeps run history for 60 days. For longer trends and analysis across the account, query the system.lakeflow tables, and join them with system.billing for cost.

questions.question: The team wants an alert whenever an important job runs much longer than its usual 30 minutes, even if it still succeeds. What should it configure?
choices: Max concurrent runs set to 1 on the job
A retry policy with 3 retries on each task
A duration warning threshold of about 45 minutes, with notifications
A timeout of 30 minutes, so that the job fails when it runs long
questions.explanation: The duration warning threshold fires a notification event when a run goes past the expected time without stopping it. A timeout, by contrast, cancels the run and marks it Timed Out.

questions.question: In a single job run with many parallel tasks, which view best shows which tasks took longest and how they overlapped?
choices: The job's Permissions page and its run-as setting
The Timeline (Gantt) view on the job run details page
The cluster's Libraries tab for each task
The Finished runs count graph on the Runs tab
questions.explanation: The Timeline view lays tasks along a time axis to show long-running tasks, dependencies, and overlap. For serverless jobs it also includes queries and their query profiles.

questions.question: A job run shows the status 'Succeeded with failures'. What does that mean?
choices: The run timed out after its leaf tasks finished
Some tasks failed, but every leaf task succeeded
The run was canceled by a user after the first task succeeded
Every task succeeded, but some retried at least once
questions.explanation: A job run's status comes from its leaf tasks. If all of them succeed while other tasks fail (for example a failure branch handled by Run if conditions), the run is Succeeded with failures.

questions.question: Task C depends on task B, and B fails. C uses the default Run if condition. Which status does C show?
choices: Timed out
Excluded
Upstream failed
Skipped by user
questions.explanation: When a task's All succeeded condition isn't met because a dependency failed, the task is marked Upstream failed. Excluded is used when conditions such as At least one failed aren't met.

questions.question: A notify_on_failure task with the Run if condition At least one failed shows 'Excluded' in a run where everything succeeded. How should this be read?
choices: As a task that failed and needs a repair run
As expected: its condition wasn't met, so it was skipped
As a configuration error that has to be fixed before the next run
As a sign that the task's compute couldn't start
questions.explanation: A task is Excluded when its Run if condition isn't met. Excluded dependencies count as successful for downstream conditions, and exclusion cascades down a linear chain of dependencies.

questions.question: A 12-task job run failed, and several downstream tasks never ran. How can the engineer find the upstream task that blocked the run?
choices: Delete the downstream tasks and re-run the job
Read the job's YAML definition to find the task with the most dependencies
Check which task has the most retries configured
In the run's Graph view, click the failed node upstream of the blocked tasks
questions.explanation: The DAG graph view shows each task's status. Clicking a node opens the task run details: the error message, output, compute, and metrics. A repair run can then re-run the failed task and its dependents.

questions.question: An on-call engineer needs an overview of recent failures across every job and pipeline in the workspace, including runs started by external orchestrators such as Airflow. Where should they look?
choices: The Runs tab under Jobs & Pipelines, filtered by status
Each job's settings page, opened one job at a time
The SQL warehouse query history for the workspace
The cluster event log of every all-purpose cluster
questions.explanation: The Runs tab gathers running and recently completed runs (from the last 60 days) for every job and pipeline you can access, and supports filtering by status, error code, run-as user, and more.

questions.question: A job is scheduled every 5 minutes, allows 1 concurrent run, and has queueing turned off. Some runs appear as 'Skipped'. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The task's Run if condition evaluated to false that time
The previous run was still active when the next was due
A user canceled those runs by hand from the UI
The job's notebook had no new data to process
questions.explanation: With the concurrency limit reached and queueing off, new runs are skipped. Turning queueing on (the default for jobs created in the UI after April 2024), raising max concurrent runs, or making each run faster would prevent it.

questions.question: In the Spark UI for a slow stage, the task summary shows a median duration of 20 seconds but a maximum of 14 minutes, and the maximum shuffle read is far larger than the median. What does this indicate, and what should be checked first?
choices: Data skew; check that AQE skew join handling is on, and consider salting
Too few shuffle partitions overall; set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 1
Driver OOM; increase spark.driver.memory and restart
Slow cluster startup; attach the job to an instance pool
questions.explanation: Skew shows up as one or a few tasks that are far larger and slower than the rest (for example, a max more than 50% above the 75th percentile). AQE (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled, on by default) splits skewed partitions in sort-merge and shuffle hash joins. Salting is the manual fallback.

questions.question: A stage's detail page shows large Spill (Memory) and Spill (Disk) values. What does that mean?
choices: Tasks ran short of execution memory and wrote data to disk
The job wrote its final output to disk instead of to Delta
The cluster lost an executor and recomputed its partitions
Data was cached in memory successfully for later reuse
questions.explanation: Spill happens when Spark doesn't have enough execution memory and moves data to disk. Fixes include more memory per core (larger or memory-optimized instances), more and smaller partitions, and reducing the data before wide operations.

questions.question: The Spark UI shows a stage writing hundreds of gigabytes of shuffle data before a join of a huge fact table with a 15 MB reference table. Which change most directly cuts the shuffle?
choices: Broadcast the small reference table so the fact table isn't shuffled
Increase the driver's memory to hold the shuffle
Run OPTIMIZE on the small reference table first
Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions so that the shuffle writes more files
questions.explanation: Large Shuffle Write and Read metrics point to expensive data movement. A broadcast hash join sends the small table to every executor, so the large side isn't shuffled at all.

questions.question: In the Spark UI, tasks in a stage show GC Time making up a large share of their duration. What does this usually indicate?
choices: There are too few files in the source table to parallelize
Photon is enabled and is slowing down garbage collection
Memory pressure on the executors, causing frequent garbage collection
The network link between the driver and cloud storage is slow
questions.explanation: High GC time means the JVM is spending its time reclaiming memory instead of doing work. Smaller partitions, more memory per core, and avoiding very wide rows or large collections in UDFs all help.

questions.question: According to the Databricks Spark UI diagnosis guide, where should you start investigating a slow Spark job?
choices: The Storage tab, to list the cached DataFrames
The Environment tab, to check every Spark property
The SQL editor's autocomplete settings
The jobs timeline, to find the longest jobs and stages
questions.explanation: The guide begins with the jobs timeline, then looks at the longest stage for skew or spill, then checks whether it is I/O bound, and then looks for other causes.

questions.question: A slow notebook runs on serverless compute, and the engineer can't find the Spark UI. What should they use instead?
choices: The Spark History Server on port 18080
The query profile for each query
The cluster's Ganglia metrics page
The driver's log4j logs
questions.explanation: Serverless compute doesn't expose the Spark UI or Spark logs. The query profile gives operator-level metrics (rows, time, spill, and so on) for diagnosing performance.

questions.question: A query against a Delta table launches thousands of tasks, each reading only a few kilobytes, and spends most of its time on overhead. What is the likely cause, and the fix?
choices: Driver OOM; collect fewer rows to the driver
Skewed join keys; salt the keys before the join
A cloud provider stockout; switch instance types
Too many small files; compact them with OPTIMIZE
questions.explanation: Small files mean many tiny tasks and a lot of metadata and listing overhead. OPTIMIZE compacts them into larger files, and on Unity Catalog managed tables predictive optimization can run OPTIMIZE automatically.

questions.question: Which statement about liquid clustering on Delta tables is correct?
choices: It works only on external tables and needs a manual ZORDER after each write
It requires the table to be partitioned by date first, then Z-ordered
It replaces partitioning and ZORDER, using CLUSTER BY on up to four columns
It automatically creates one directory per distinct clustering key value, like Hive partitions
questions.explanation: Liquid clustering is a flexible layout technique. Use CREATE TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (cols), or ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY on an existing table, with up to four clustering keys. It isn't compatible with partitioning or ZORDER.

questions.question: Query patterns have changed, and a liquid-clustered table should now be clustered by customer_id instead of order_date. What happens when the engineer runs ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY (customer_id)?
choices: The table is converted back to Hive-style partitioning on customer_id
The command fails, because clustering keys are fixed once the table is created
Existing data isn't rewritten; new writes and OPTIMIZE use the new keys
The entire table is rewritten immediately and synchronously
questions.explanation: A key benefit of liquid clustering is that clustering keys can be redefined without rewriting existing data, so the layout can evolve with query patterns. ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY NONE turns clustering off.

questions.question: How is data in a liquid-clustered table actually reclustered?
choices: VACUUM reclusters the data each time it removes old files
ANALYZE TABLE reorders the data files based on the statistics it collects
Clustering happens only when the table is dropped and recreated
OPTIMIZE reclusters incrementally, and OPTIMIZE FULL reclusters every record
questions.explanation: Liquid clustering is incremental: OPTIMIZE rewrites only the data that needs it. OPTIMIZE FULL forces a full recluster, for example after the keys change. Writes above size thresholds can also be clustered as they happen.

questions.question: An engineer wants Databricks to choose and adapt a table's clustering keys automatically based on its query history. What is required?
choices: PARTITIONED BY AUTO on a Hive metastore table with ZORDER
ZORDER BY AUTO, together with a weekly OPTIMIZE job
CLUSTER BY AUTO on a managed table with predictive optimization
CLUSTER BY AUTO on any external Parquet table in a volume
questions.explanation: Automatic liquid clustering picks keys and runs the clustering through predictive optimization. It is available only on Unity Catalog managed Delta (and Iceberg v3) tables.

questions.question: Which statement about predictive optimization is correct?
choices: It automatically runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and ANALYZE on managed tables, on serverless compute
It rewrites queries at runtime to use broadcast joins, at no extra cost
It applies only to external tables, and it runs on the customer's all-purpose clusters
It runs only when a user calls the PREDICT OPTIMIZE command on a table
questions.explanation: Predictive optimization removes the need to schedule maintenance by hand. It decides when OPTIMIZE (which includes clustering), VACUUM, and ANALYZE are worthwhile for Unity Catalog managed tables, and runs them on serverless compute billed under a serverless jobs SKU. External tables are not covered.

questions.question: Predictive optimization should be enabled for every managed table in the sales catalog except those in sales.sandbox, and the operations it performs need to be monitored. What should the engineer do?
choices: ENABLE it on the catalog, DISABLE it on sales.sandbox, and query its system table
Enable it on each table separately, because it can't be inherited, and use DESCRIBE HISTORY
Run OPTIMIZE sales.* every hour from a job, and check the job's run history
Set spark.databricks.predictiveOptimization = true on every cluster, and read the driver logs
questions.explanation: Predictive optimization can be enabled, disabled, or inherited at the account, catalog, schema, and table levels (ALTER CATALOG | SCHEMA | TABLE ... ENABLE | DISABLE | INHERIT PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION), and children inherit from their parents. Its operations and costs are recorded in system.storage.predictive_optimization_operations_history.

questions.question: A classic cluster fails to start with the termination reason INIT_SCRIPT_FAILURE. What should the engineer do first?
choices: Read the init script logs, then fix the script or its path
Turn on Photon, which skips the init scripts during startup
Contact the cloud provider to request more instance quota
Raise the Spark driver memory and restart the cluster
questions.explanation: Init scripts run on every node, so a failure on any node stops the cluster from launching. The cause is either that the script couldn't be fetched (wrong path or no permission) or that it ran and exited non-zero. A failing global init script shows as GLOBAL_INIT_SCRIPT_FAILURE.

questions.question: A cluster won't launch, and the event log shows that the cloud provider couldn't allocate the requested VM size in the zone (a stockout), or that a quota was exceeded. Which actions are appropriate?
choices: Raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and restart the cluster
Change the notebook's default language to SQL
Reinstall all of the cluster's libraries and restart
Try another instance type or zone, or request a quota increase
questions.explanation: Launch failures such as CLOUD_PROVIDER_RESOURCE_STOCKOUT, quota errors, and CLOUD_PROVIDER_LAUNCH_FAILURE are problems on the infrastructure side. The cluster event log shows the error code. Fixes include retrying, alternative instance types or zones, enabling flexible node types (an automatic fallback to compatible instance types), quota increases, or a larger subnet.

questions.question: Version 1.5 of a library is installed as a cluster library, and a notebook runs %pip install mylib==2.0. Which version does that notebook use, and does it affect other notebooks on the cluster?
choices: The install fails, because the two versions can't coexist on one cluster
2.0 in that notebook only; other notebooks keep using 1.5
The notebook uses 1.5, because cluster libraries always win
Every notebook on the cluster switches to 2.0
questions.explanation: Precedence, highest first: libraries in the current working directory (Git folders), then the Git folder root, then notebook-scoped libraries (%pip), then cluster libraries, then the libraries bundled with Databricks Runtime. Notebook-scoped libraries are isolated to that notebook's session.

questions.question: Halfway through a session, a notebook upgrades a package with %pip install, but import still returns the old version that was loaded earlier. What should the engineer run?
choices: %sh pip uninstall pyspark
dbutils.library.restartPython()
dbutils.fs.refreshMounts()
spark.catalog.clearCache()
questions.explanation: A package that is already imported stays loaded in the Python process. Restarting the Python process (dbutils.library.restartPython()) picks up the newly installed version. Putting %pip commands at the top of the notebook avoids the problem.

questions.question: A job fails with 'Driver is temporarily unavailable', and the event log shows Driver_Not_Responding with a message about GC. The notebook calls toPandas() on a large DataFrame. What is the best fix?
choices: Stop pulling large results to the driver, or use a larger driver
Enable the deletion vectors feature on the table
Add more worker nodes, which share the driver's memory load
Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 1 for the job
questions.explanation: collect() and toPandas() bring all of the data onto the driver, which causes OOM or long GC pauses. Workers don't add driver memory. Keep the work distributed, or size the driver for what truly has to run there.

questions.question: A few executor tasks fail with OutOfMemoryError during a large join, while most tasks finish without trouble. Which response best targets the root cause?
choices: Lower spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 1 KB
Raise spark.driver.memory, because executor tasks run on the driver
Fix the skewed partitions with AQE or salting, or use more partitions
Turn off adaptive query execution to keep partition sizes predictable
questions.explanation: Executor OOM in only a few tasks usually means some partitions are far too large (skew). Spreading the data more evenly, or giving each task more memory, addresses the cause. Driver memory has nothing to do with executor tasks.

questions.question: What happens to the data files when a Unity Catalog managed table is dropped?
choices: They are deleted after a recovery period (7 days by default)
The files stay in cloud storage forever and must be deleted by hand
The files are deleted instantly and can never be recovered
The files are moved to an external location named by the table owner
questions.explanation: For managed tables, Unity Catalog owns the data lifecycle. A dropped table can be recovered for 7 days by default (configurable from 0 hours to 30 days) before an automated purge removes its files.
